title: Intermittency in Wind-Driven Fires
authors: Laurent Hébert-Dufresne, Aanjaneya Kumar, S. Redner
abstract: We construct a wind-driven forest-fire model in one dimension in which a fire can jump gaps between trees to ignite disjoint downwind forests. The size of a gap that a fire can jump depends on the fire intensity, which increases as the fire propagates through trees and diminishes as the fire jumps gaps. Trees grow on empty sites at rate $r$ and lightning strikes each site with rate $f$. When $f\ll r/L$, where $L$ is the system length, lightning is sufficiently rare that quasi-deterministic dynamics arises where all trees are consumed when a lightning-induced fire occurs. For $f\gg L^{-μ}$ with $μ\approx 0.8$, lightning is sufficiently frequent that a steady state is reached, but with unexpected behaviors for the forest- and gap-size distributions. Intermittency arises in between these regimes, with coexisting temporal domains of deterministic and chaotic dynamics.
summary: This paper models wind-driven forest fires in 1D, revealing three distinct dynamical regimes governed by lightning frequency. It demonstrates that the intermediate regime exhibits intermittency, characterized by alternating periods of stable growth and chaotic, catastrophic events. The work provides quantitative scaling laws for fire sizes and gap distributions in this complex non-equilibrium system.
main_problem: The paper investigates the complex dynamics, particularly intermittency, in a one-dimensional model of wind-driven forest fires.
main_result: The model exhibits three distinct regimes controlled by the lightning rate, showing power-law scaling for gap sizes and evidence of coexisting deterministic and chaotic dynamics in the intermittent regime.
method: The dynamics are analyzed by constructing a 1D forest-fire model and studying the time evolution of tree density and fire propagation under varying rates of tree growth and lightning strikes.
model_or_system: The system is a 1D periodic ring representing a forest, where sites can be empty or occupied by a tree. Fire propagation is governed by an intensity mechanism that increases within a forest and decreases when jumping gaps. The dynamics are driven by tree growth (rate r) and random lightning strikes (rate f).
key_observables: Tree density $ho(t)$, fire and gap size distributions, time interval distribution $Q(\Delta t)$ between catastrophes, and characteristic fire sizes.
important_parameters: Tree growth rate ($r$), lightning strike rate ($f$), and the system length ($L$). Key regimes are defined by the relative magnitudes of $f$ compared to $r/L$ and $L^{-\mu}$.
main_assumptions: The model is treated as one-dimensional and periodic. The analysis relies on identifying distinct dynamical regimes based on the frequency of external forcing (lightning).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the time evolution of tree density across the three regimes (quasi-deterministic, steady state, intermittent). They also show the distribution of fire sizes and the probability distribution of time intervals between major fire events.
paper_structure: The paper analyzes the system across three regimes defined by the lightning rate $f$: quasi-deterministic (rare lightning), steady state (frequent lightning), and the intermediate intermittent regime. The analysis focuses on characterizing the scaling laws and underlying dynamics in each regime.
why_interesting: The study of intermittency and the transition between different dynamical regimes (deterministic vs. chaotic) in a non-equilibrium system is highly relevant to understanding complex, self-organizing phenomena in physics, analogous to pattern formation or driven many-body systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Wind-driven forest fire model. Each row shows the system state after each forest has burned. After the lightning strike on the second tree of a forest of size 4, a fire of intensity 3 is created. The numbers indicate the fire intensity at each site. The fire jumps the first gap because its intensity exceeds the gap length. The fire stops when its intensity reaches zero.

FIG. 2: Spacetime plots of tree dynamics on a ring of length L = 104. (a) Lightning rate f = 10−4, which corresponds to the quasi-deterministic regime. (b) f = 2×10−1, which corre- sponds to the steady state. (c) f = 10−2, which corresponds to the intermittent regime. The upper curve in each panel shows the time dependence of the tree density. The bottom plots show the local tree density over space estimated with a running average over windows of length 100 at fixed time intervals.

FIG. 3: The distribution of the log of the fire sizes (red) and gap sizes (green) for systems of different sizes L and different lighting rates f. The data are scaled so that k = 1 corresponds to a size of L/2 and then smoothed by logarithmic binning. The gap size distribution in the intermittent regime is a robust power-law distribution with scaling exponent close to −3.

FIG. 4: Characteristic fire size, excluding catastrophes. The stars indicate the peak fire size as inferred from a parabolic fit to the curves near the maximum. Insets show the peak fire size (top right, fit with 0.07L+0.74) and the corresponding value of f (bottom left, fit with 10.9L−0.68) as a function of system size L. Both fits have error bars of 0.02.
FIG. 5: The probability distribution Q(∆t) of the time in- tervals ∆t between catastrophes for the case of L = 105 and f = 3 × 10−3.
